topic.title: Translating your documentation with Content Fusion

body.p: Leveraging AI, Content Fusion can translate your documentation automatically. But even with AI, no translation can be right without the context that surrounds it: the words your product actually shows on screen, the terms your team has settled on, the typographic conventions of the target language. What follows is a journal of translating our own user guide into French, and the fine-tuning that turned out to be necessary.
body.note: The feature is marked Experimental in the UI. The workflow below is stable; expect the defaults to keep improving.

section.title: Step 1: Three clicks for a full translation
section.p: In your project workspace, open Translation Jobs, choose New translation, pick your publications and your target languages, and start the job. Publications are a multi-select grouped by language, so you can see which languages each one already exists in; target languages come from a list, or you can type any BCP-47 tag you need (pt-PT, fr-CA). Two publications and three languages is six translations from one job.

An AI agent then walks each DITA map, translates every topic, and writes a parallel language folder per target. The job's Bring into Workspace action brings those folders into your workspace, where they are ordinary files to review and commit. The publication's deliverables are mirrored for the new language too, so the translation is publishable straight away, with no manual ditaProject.xml editing.

Re-running is cheap, which matters more than it sounds. Content Fusion keeps a translation index at .contentfusion/i18n/translation-index.xml, pairing each source file with the translation made from it, and skips the files that haven't changed since. So the working rhythm becomes: write English, translate, import, commit. To force a full re-translation, delete the target files or the index.

section.title: Step 2: Review — not quite right
section.p: Our first run was a four-topic guide into French with the instructions field left empty, and on its own terms it read well: agreement, register and sentence structure nearly all correct, headings in sentence case instead of mirroring English Title Case, code and file paths untouched. A native speaker proofreading those files in isolation would have approved them.

We pointed a model at the translated files together with the English source and our own UI resource bundle, and asked what was wrong. Then a human reviewer made their own pass and checked the AI's list. What came out:

ul.li: Terminology that contradicted our own product. Content Fusion ships a French UI — 1818 strings across six locales, in a file the agent never saw. So the guide told French users to click Validations entrantes when the button reads Commits entrants, and called their role Réviseur when the product says Examinateur. Eight terms, around twenty occurrences.

One term, several renderings. dépôt six times in one topic, référentiel twice in the next, and never mixed inside a single file. Every file was internally consistent and disagreed with its neighbour, which is the signature of how the run is parallelized: one sub-agent per file, each blind to its siblings' decisions. Every file gets its own private dialect.

No French typography. French puts a non-breaking space before : ; ! ? and inside « ». The tree contained zero U+00A0 characters across 11 places that needed one, and with a plain space the renderer can orphan the colon onto the next line.
Emphasis drift. <b> was widened to swallow the words around it, differently in each file.
A product name left in English — Software Docs Starter — even though the product ships a French name for it, plus an agreement error inside an <indexterm> in one of two parallel topics.

section.p: The terminology mismatches were the important find, because they generalize past our product: the AI can write beautiful French and still be wrong about your software. The words on your screens are a fact, not an inference, and only someone with the product open in one window and the manual in the other catches the difference.

Last but not least, the prose was grammatically correct and still didn't read like French written by a French technical writer. It read like a translation — literal where a native speaker would have reached for the ordinary word. Our clearest example: bande is a strip of material, while a strip in a UI is a bandeau. Nothing a grammar check flags, and nothing a reader of the French guide fails to notice.

section.title: Step 3: Fine-tuning
section.p: Every pass re-translates every file, and translation costs tokens. So rather than iterate against the real guide, we cut a publication down to four topics and developed against that. The defects we were hunting are systematic, so four topics expose them as readily as two hundred.

li.p: Added a ui-glossary-fr-FR.md file in the .contentfusion/i18n/ directory, holding the shipped English→French strings from our application. The agent is sandboxed to your DITA workspace and cannot reach into your application's repository, so you have to bring the strings to it.

Building it is a one-pass job for any LLM: hand over your resource bundle and the target locale, and ask for English -> target pairs, labels only. Two things are worth getting right. Filter rather than dumping the raw bundle — ours is 16,400 lines and roughly 250k tokens, so the read gets truncated and the agent carries on believing it consulted the authority; filtered to buttons, fields, views, tabs, dialogs, roles and product terms it's about 920 pairs and 13k tokens. And check the count, because a filter that can silently drop rows will drop the irregular ones, and the irregular ones are the interesting ones.
The result is unremarkable to look at, which is the point:
li.codeblock:
## Not translated by the product — shown in English - `DITA Map` (key `ditamap`) - `Org-level role` (key `organization.role`)
## Labels - `Add reviewer` -> `Ajouter un examinateur` - `Incoming commits` -> `Commits entrants` - `Repository` -> `Dépôt` - `Software Docs Starter` -> `Documentation logicielle - Guide de démarrage` - `Workspace` -> `Espace de travail`
li.p: That first list earns its place as much as the pairs do. Ours marks 18 labels as not translated for French, meaning the running French UI shows English for them — so the manual has to as well.

Added agent-instructions.md next to it, telling the agent about the glossary and about the rules that are specific to French. This file applies to every translation in the project, unlike the per-job Translation Instructions field; where the two contradict each other, the field wins. The New translation dialog has a callout that creates the file for you from a commented template. Write plain language — the agent reads it verbatim before it starts.
Five rules earned their place, plus one about tone:

The shipped UI is the authority. This is the rule the glossary exists for, and it is permanent — a fact about your product rather than a limitation of the tool. Relative links are resolved for you, so naming the file is enough:
li.codeblock: ### Terminology — the shipped UI is the authority .contentfusion/i18n/ui-glossary-fr-FR.md holds the product's shipped en→fr UI strings. Read it before translating. Any text inside `<uicontrol>` or `<menucascade>`, and every button, field, view, page, and role name, must reuse the shipped French string verbatim. Never invent a French label that contradicts a shipped one. If a label is absent from the glossary, translate it once and reuse that exact rendering everywhere.

li.p: Frozen terms. Decide the answer yourself instead of asking every worker to arrive at the same one, and name the plausible-but-wrong rendering explicitly — the negatives are what stop it:
li.codeblock: - repository → le dépôt — never référentiel - workspace → l'espace de travail - reviewer → l'examinateur — never réviseur - incoming commits → les commits entrants — never validations entrantes - DITA Map → DITA Map (the French UI leaves it in English)

li.p: Delegation, which is what stops each file from inventing its own dialect:
li.codeblock: ### Delegation Translate clusters of semantically related topics (e.g. chapters, sub-chapters) in a single "dita-translator" sub-agent.
li.p: Cluster related topics rather than demanding the whole publication in one worker. A single worker holding every topic buys consistency, but it serializes the run and risks running short of context; chapter-sized batches are the middle ground.
French typography, which the baseline had none of:
li.codeblock: ### French typography Use a non-breaking space (U+00A0) before `:` `;` `!` `?` and inside `« »`. Never a plain space.

li.p: Inline markup fidelity, for the emphasis drift:
li.codeblock: ### Inline markup fidelity Preserve the exact scope of every inline element. The words emphasized in the source must be the words emphasized in the target — never widen ``/`` to swallow an article, preposition, or the surrounding phrase, and never narrow it. `Author platform user role` → `rôle d'utilisateur de la plateforme Auteur`, not `rôle d'utilisateur … Auteur`.

ol.li:
And also mentioned that we want the translation to read as natural French, something a native speaker would write:Translate this into [language]. Make it sound natural to a native speaker, not literal. Keep the same meaning and tone. Give me the best version and briefly explain any important nuance.
An instruction like this sets the register, but it does not fix individual slips. Pair it with a style-notes section that names the ones you have actually seen: write natural French changes nothing, while bande is a strip of material; a UI strip is bandeau changes the output.

li.note: Proofread your literal examples character by character, because they carry more weight than your prose. In our German glossary the header stated the quotation-mark rule correctly and then demonstrated it with an ASCII " as the closing character instead of „'s partner “ (U+201E opening, U+201C closing). The agent followed the example rather than the sentence, and every quoted label in the German output shipped wrong — something the uninstructed baseline had got right. A bad instruction is worse than no instruction, and it fails uniformly across every file, which makes it harder to catch in review rather than easier.

li.p: Ran the translation on the four topics again and reviewed it with AI a second time. Same agent, same model, same topics — the only change was those two files in the workspace:

strow.stentry: Software Docs Starter left in English
Same term rendered differently per file

li.p: Worth noting what is not in that table: the XML itself was never the problem. Both runs matched the element inventory of the English source and were well-formed throughout. Every defect we found was lexical or typographic, which tells you where to spend your review effort.

section.p: One regression is worth reporting, because it is the kind you would not predict. Our English source has a defect — a ( that never closes. The baseline quietly repaired it. The instructed run, told to preserve the source structure faithfully, moved the parenthesis and left it open, so the output shipped the bug. Tightening the instructions costs you the model's free proofreading. Fix your source instead of relying on it.
section.note: Our measurements cover one four-topic publication and one model, and they compare two DITA outputs rather than two fresh human reviews. We haven't yet measured against a large publication, where the delegation rule in particular has more room to matter.

section.title: Step 4: Translate the full user guide
section.p: With agent-instructions.md and the glossary committed to the workspace, the real run needs nothing new: point a translation job at the full publication and let it work through the map. From there you are back in the rhythm from step 1 — write English, translate, import, review, commit — and the translation index means each later run only touches the topics you changed.

For the next language, copy the structure and not the text. Generate a glossary for the new locale, keep the delegation and markup-fidelity rules as they are, and write typography, frozen terms and register from scratch. Note that agent-instructions.md is a single fixed path that every target language reads, so name the language in each heading — ### French typography, not ### Typography. That naming is not cosmetic: French wants a non-breaking space before : and German wants no space at all, so a rule you assumed was universal will corrupt the second language you add.

Above all, don't assume the vocabulary transfers. Working from the same resource bundle, our French UI renders Repository as Dépôt while the German keeps Repository; French keeps DITA Map in English while German writes DITA-Map. The two locales don't even agree on which labels stay in English: 18 are marked do-not-translate for French, 13 for German, and only 8 in both. You look this up per language, or you get it wrong, which is exactly why the glossary step exists.

And keep growing the instructions from what you observe. Every line in ours exists because a specific defect happened, and that is the part worth copying: write down observed mistakes, not general advice. Start the style-notes section empty and add to it after each run.
